item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03494-1 Chromosome-scale genome sequences from across the barley genus Hordeum reveal large structural variation, evidence of ancient genetic exchange and extensive divergence of regulatory sequences. These evolutionary processes have generated diversity that could be used to improve cultivated barley.

item.title: Nature: Pockets in compacted DNA tune gene activation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03492-3 The stochastic activation of specific genes is needed for the proper formation of neuronal circuits. Opposing forces act on inactive DNA to balance this process.

item.title: Nature: Bogong moths can migrate using an internal geomagnetic compass
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03693-w Australian migratory moths navigate long distances, in part owing to a stellar ‘compass’. It transpires that they have another compass that detects the inclination, or angle, of Earth’s magnetic field lines and that probably relies on a light-dependent quantum-mechanical mechanism similar to the one found in night-migratory songbirds.

item.title: Nature: Dengue has exploded globally with shocking speed
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03813-6 The number of recorded cases of the mosquito-borne disease worldwide rose by a factor of 34 over 34 years.

item.title: Nature: Enzymatic reactions adapted to make ‘living’ chains of sugars
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03382-8 By tuning the binding between enzymes that chain sugars together and the molecules that initiate the reaction, precise chain lengths have been made for biological studies.

item.title: Nature: An enduring climatic burden from past peatland drainage
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 Reconstruction of radiative forcing resulting from worldwide peatland drainage over the past two centuries reveals a persistent net warming effect caused by the dominant forcing of drainage-induced CO2 emissions over that of avoided CH4 emissions.

item.title: Nature: Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11275-z A multi-omic gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility map of human coronary artery disease provides a framework for mapping disease-associated genetic variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

item.title: Nature: Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11301-0 Architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer drive cell state diversification through mechanochemical reprogramming of stem cell identities.

item.title: Nature: A gut–brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11315-8 In flies, sugar-sensing enteric neurons activate brain neurons that inhibit crop duct motor neurons, relaxing the foregut muscles to facilitate food transfer to the crop, which sustains ingestion and regulates food intake.

item.title: Nature: Quantum-enhanced sensing with 500 photons via Fock-space confocal focusing
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11353-2 Quantum confocal microscopy enables deterministic preparation of high-photon-number Fock-like states with up to 500 photons, reducing photon-number variance by 21.5 dB and achieving record displacement-sensing precision 19.2 dB beyond the standard quantum limit.

item.title: Nature: Licensing mechanisms during RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CAST

item.title: Nature: Middle–Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11341-6 Dental morphology and proteomic analyses of fossils from southern China identify lineages with and without Denisovan affinity, indicating the diversity of hominin populations in this region in the Middle to Late Pleistocene.

item.title: Nature: Sustainable cement production via a liquid-phase pathway
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11313-w Sustainable cement production can be achieved by accelerating its reaction kinetics through a microwave carbon-plasma method, reducing the standard processing time from hours to seconds.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11304-x An enzymatic method for making high-molecular-weight polysaccharides in a way similar to synthetic polymerization techniques, rather than biosynthetically, is presented.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11311-y Interrogation of the clustered protocadherin locus shows an unexpected ability of genes to transcribe within a seemingly silent chromatin environment.

item.title: Nature: Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11345-2 Analysis of exomes from over 1.4 million participants implicates 207 genes, including large effect coding variants and gene burden tests, and demonstrates the utility of large-scale sequencing for trait prediction and variant interpretation.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains
item.description: Nearly one in three older adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders takes potentially harmful medications that can worsen brain function and increase the risk of hospitalization and premature death. Despite encouraging progress over the past decade, researchers warn that medication-related harm remains a major and potentially preventable threat to healthy aging.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
item.description: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
item.description: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
item.description: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

item.title: ScienceDaily: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
item.description: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
item.description: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
item.description: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang
item.description: A surprising discovery by MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists reveals that Einstein’s famous theory of particle motion misses something important when particles travel near the speed of light. Their new calculations show that heavy quarks moving through an ultra-hot plasma experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein’s traditional model cannot fully explain.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
item.description: A common antibody in the gut may be a powerful natural defense against colon cancer, with researchers finding that mice lacking it developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, revealing a promising new avenue for preventing cancer before it starts.

item.description: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to…

item.title: ScienceDaily: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
item.description: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

item.description: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

item.title: New Scientist: Toddlers form complex memories but may then lose access to them
item.description: Few of us can remember events from our earliest years, but that might be because we lose the ability to recall memories - not because we didn't make them in the first place
